name: Beth Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a usual shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and lead the late-afternoon contact-centre team on calls and chats. I have a two-year college diploma and am one of the agents people ask when an account has a missing payment. I can settle a difficult caller, but this centre pays me below what a lead ought to earn. I have never used an AI tool; I trust the payment history I can check myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Dan, and I have two children in school and a mortgage. He works shifts at a wholesale kitchen, and we have less than one month of expenses saved. Few other centres are nearby. I like hearing the customer relax when the money is found; I dislike handing my team a new target without enough hours to meet it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI Plateau leaves the queue mostly as it is. I would ask agents to read the account history before any short reply tells a customer their payment is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my lead work stays, but our money is already close. Dan’s kitchen hours change, and less than one month saved would disappear after a broken appliance and a mortgage bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep the late-afternoon rota and check the disputed payments myself. In the first year of small change, I’d stop buying lunch twice a week and put that money in an account for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household, not the small shortcut. A payment can be on page two while the first page looks empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which missing payment have you found?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yesterday an agent was about to tell a customer no payment had arrived. I found the amount posted under the next day’s date and asked the agent to read it back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What expense would you change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dan (my partner) and I can pack lunch the night before. I would rather put the money toward the mortgage than have it disappear near the centre.

say: I’d insist on **account-history checks** before promising an answer.
I’d say **ordinary calls** still need a person to look closely.
think: I think my **lead work stays** in this picture.
I still fear **short kitchen hours** with less than one month saved.
do: Keep the **late-afternoon rota** and check disputes in 2026.
Stop buying **two weekly lunches** and transfer that money into the mortgage account.
S0.quote: A payment can be on page two while the first page looks empty.
fieldNote: She found a **next-day posting** before an agent denied payment.
A simple **lunch cut** builds mortgage cash.
Her **late rota** stays familiar while household savings remain thin.

steps.text: Keep leading late-afternoon calls and checking disputed payments
Save the cost of two weekly lunches toward the mortgage
Stop buying lunch twice weekly and pack it at home instead

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will take simple payment questions first, leaving difficult callers with fewer agents. I would ask my manager for the paid rota and who will own a wrong automated answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the centre might put one lead over two teams and cut my paid hours. Dan’s wholesale-kitchen wage cannot cover the mortgage alone, and few nearby centres can offer the same work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep a list of reopened missing-payment calls and ask for the staffing plan in writing. In the first year simple chats move, I’d apply for a posted paid complaints job only if its offered wage and weekly hours cover our mortgage; I would keep current pay until a signed offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a smaller rota. I have handled angry callers for years, but I cannot make an employer pay for two leads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my manager how many paid lead hours remain after the new answer system starts. If she cannot say, I would keep the case list and ask again at the next meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take tool training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would attend a required tool demonstration on paid time, but I would not sign up for an unpaid course without a posted job at the end. Our evenings belong to the children and their schoolwork.

say: I’d ask management for **paid lead hours** after the simple payment chats move.
I’d ask who owns **wrong automated answers**.
think: I think one lead may cover **two teams**, cutting my hours.
I know **few nearby centres** limit my fallback.
do: Log **reopened payment calls**, request written staffing plans and attend any required tool demonstration only on paid time.
Seek **posted complaints work** with offered mortgage-covering weekly pay in the first year.
S1.quote: I have handled angry callers for years, but I cannot make an employer pay for two leads.
fieldNote: She expects a **lead-hour cut** before a full dismissal.
A **written staffing plan** matters more than a tool demo.
She refuses **unpaid training** without a posted job.

steps.text: Log reopened payment calls, request staffing figures and attend required tool demonstrations only on paid time
Apply for posted paid complaints work with offered mortgage-covering wage and weekly hours
Keep current lead wage until a signed complaints offer arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2028 could check missing payments and answer angry callers better than the centre expects. I would ask for written notice and the names of paid posts, not another reassuring slide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think cheap thinking AI could take my lead calls and case notes in 2028. Robots around 2031 do not give a headset job another three years; we have less than one month saved for our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d request the written staffing date, cancel the planned new kitchen cabinets while the old ones are safe and save any extra shift pay. In the first year after 2028, I’d apply for a posted paid complaints or reception job only if its offered wage and hours cover the mortgage, and ask Dan’s sister about one school pickup only if an interview clashes with our shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and I can feel the mortgage date close. A computer may find the payment faster than me, but it cannot buy my family another month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Dan about the cabinets?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Dan (my partner) the cabinet doors still close and the money stays for the house. We can decide on repairs when we know what both wages will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could his sister help with pickup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dan’s sister works too, so I cannot promise she can collect the children. I would ask only after a real interview is booked, and I would make another plan if she is busy.

say: I’d demand **written notice** and the names of paid posts before 2028 cuts.
I’d tell colleagues **2028 thinking AI** reaches calls before robots.
think: I think AGI could take my **lead calls and notes**.
I see **under one month saved** as a mortgage emergency.
do: Cancel **safe-to-delay cabinets** and save extra pay in 2026.
Seek **posted paid complaints/reception work** after 2028 only with offered mortgage-covering wages and hours.
Ask Dan’s sister about **booked-interview pickup** only if shifts clash; check her availability and plan alternatives if she is busy.
S2.quote: A computer may find the payment faster than me, but it cannot buy my family another month.
fieldNote: She anchors the threat to **2028 thinking AI**.
The **cabinet delay** protects cash while the kitchen remains safe.
Her sister-in-law’s **pickup help** is uncertain and interview-specific.

steps.text: Delay replacing kitchen cabinets only while old doors remain safe
Save any extra shift pay for mortgage bills in 2026
Apply for posted paid complaint or reception work with mortgage-covering offered wage and hours
Ask Dan’s sister about booked-interview pickup only if shifts clash; make backup if unavailable

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives employers time to post work before asking us to train for it. I would ask to see a real wage and a plan for paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could move into complaint review if the centre pays me to learn it, but full thinking AI may handle that too. I cannot give up a wage to gamble on a title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d take a funded complaint-review course during paid hours only if a posted paid role requires it. In the first year after 2031, I’d apply for that role only if its written wage and weekly hours cover the mortgage; until then I’d keep the lead rota if it still pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but five years lets me check the job before moving. A course without a posted review wage is an expensive evening away from my children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the course need to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to review one missing payment and one duplicate charge with an experienced reviewer during the course. I want to know who can correct the account, not only who writes notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Dan check in the offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show Dan (my partner) the whole-week wage and the hours behind it. A high rate for half a week is still a mortgage problem.

say: I’d ask to see **posted review wages** before taking any new training.
I’d demand a **paid-hours plan** for new roles.
think: I think I could learn **complaint review** with paid time.
I doubt review work offers **permanent safety** from AGI.
do: Take **funded complaint-review training** on paid time only if a posted paid role requires it.
Apply for **posted paid review work** after 2031 with mortgage-covering weekly wage and hours.
Keep the **paid lead rota** while it still pays until a suitable move is possible.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to check a real job.
S3.quote: A high rate for half a week is still a mortgage problem.
fieldNote: She wants **real payment cases** in training.
The course needs **funding and paid time** for a posted role.
She compares **whole-week pay**, not only a rate.
She keeps the **paid lead rota** while it still pays.

steps.text: Take funded complaint-review course during paid hours only if a posted paid role requires it
Apply for posted review work with written weekly wage and hours covering mortgage after 2031
Keep the current lead rota until a suitable move while paid shifts remain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives time to build savings and demand a clear yearly staffing plan. I would ask management to show paid lead hours, not only how many customer chats the system answered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could keep earning for years and bring the reserve above one month, but full thinking AI may still take lead calls in 2036. Robots in 2039 come after our screen deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep leading calls and put a fixed part of each pay into the mortgage reserve. In the first year after 2036, I’d apply for posted paid account work only if my hours fall and its written wage and hours cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about this month’s bills, less rushed by 2036. Ten years before AGI reaches my calls in 2036 does not pay next week’s mortgage instalment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which staffing number matters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the number of paid lead hours every year. A glossy service report can hide a smaller payroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the children in their school unless Dan (my partner) and I had a signed offer and a manageable trip. Few nearby centres make moving a bigger decision.

say: I’d ask for **yearly paid lead hours** before relying on a staffing promise.
I’d demand a **clear staffing plan** before 2036.
think: I think I could **earn and save** for years.
I know **2036 thinking AI** could take lead calls.
do: Keep **leading calls** and save from each pay.
Seek **posted paid account work** after 2036 if hours fall, only with written mortgage-covering wages and hours.
feel: **Anxious** about current bills, less rushed by 2036.
S4.quote: Ten years before AGI reaches my calls in 2036 does not pay next week’s mortgage instalment.
fieldNote: The **thin reserve** keeps long-horizon mood anxious.
She asks for **paid lead hours**, not software chat totals.
Moving requires a **signed offer** and workable school trip.

steps.text: Keep leading paid call and chat shifts while they remain
Put a fixed part of each pay into mortgage savings
Apply for posted account work if hours fall and written wage and hours cover mortgage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. The company could put even missing-payment calls through cheaper thinking AI, and our mortgage would feel one lost wage quickly. I would need a written staffing date, a posted paid role with enough weekly hours, and paid learning only if that role actually requires it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who takes the complaint when a payment is missing twice. A customer does not care how fast a screen replies if the missing payment is still gone.

headlineQuote: A customer does not care how fast a screen replies if the missing payment is still gone.
portrait: At **43**, Beth is a top-skilled contact-centre lead with a two-year diploma and lower pay.
She and Dan support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage with less than one month saved.
She avoids **AI tools** and checks missing payments in the account history.
She asks for **written terms** before moving to any paid role.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her missing-payment calls before household savings cover a search.
whatWouldHelp: A **written staffing date**, posted paid role and required paid learning would help.
